original_value: We examine the role of political ideology in portfolio formation by studying a unique set of investors whose ideology can be precisely captured by a well-defined, continuous measure and whose personal asset allocation decisions are mandatorily disclosed, namely, the members of the U.S. Congress. As such, we overcome important methodological issues facing previous work in this area. We find that politicians with similar beliefs hold similar portfolios and that more liberal members engage in more socially responsible investing (SRI), even within political parties. Politicians disproportionately favor the SRI categories that reflect their favorite issues, while salience plays an important role in activating their ideologically based preferences for SRI. In addition, more ideological investors are less likely to engage in quid pro quo behavior. We conclude that ideology is a pervasive psychological factor that governs decisions across the domains of politics, investing, and, even, ethics.  This paper was accepted by Lauren Cohen, finance.

result.paraphrase: We study how political ideology shapes portfolio formation using a distinctive group of investors whose ideology is precisely measured on a well-defined continuous scale and whose personal asset allocation choices must be disclosed: members of the U.S. Congress. This lets us address major methodological problems in earlier research on the topic. We find that politicians with similar beliefs tend to hold similar portfolios, and that more liberal members invest more in socially responsible investing (SRI), including within parties. Politicians disproportionately choose the SRI categories tied to their preferred issues, and issue salience strongly activates these ideology-driven SRI preferences. We also find that more ideological investors are less likely to engage in quid pro quo behavior. Overall, we conclude that ideology is a pervasive psychological force shaping decisions in politics, investing, and ethics. This paper was accepted by Lauren Cohen, finance.
